summary: Specifies how to encapsulate and transmit IPv4, IPv6, and ARP packets over InfiniBand. It describes the link-layer address used when resolving IP addresses in IPoIB subnets and how IP multicast addresses map to InfiniBand multicast addresses. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: IPoIB defines how IPv4, IPv6, and ARP packets travel over InfiniBand. It also explains how InfiniBand links, addresses, and multicast groups are set up for IP traffic.

questions: what is the mtu for ip over infiniband
how does ip multicast map to infiniband
what is the ipoib link layer address
subtitle: How IP and ARP packets use InfiniBand unreliable datagrams, addresses, and multicast groups.

tldr.problem: IP needs a defined way to use InfiniBand, whose link is a configured group of members rather than a physical Ethernet segment.
tldr.mechanism: IPoIB uses InfiniBand Unreliable Datagram mode, adds a four-octet protocol header, and defines link addresses, multicast mappings, and link setup.
tldr.outcome: IPv4, IPv6, and ARP can use InfiniBand links with shared rules for addressing and multicast. RFC 4391 is updated by RFC 8064.

today: RFC 4391 is a Proposed Standard, published in April 2006, and is updated by RFC 8064. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: IP over Unreliable Datagram Mode
sections.content:
InfiniBand supports several transport modes. RFC 4391 specifies IP over Unreliable Datagram (UD) mode because all InfiniBand elements support it and it provides multicast, partitioning, and a 32-bit CRC.

All IPoIB implementations MUST support IP over UD. Other InfiniBand transport modes are outside the scope of this specification. The RFC describes link setup, address resolution, packet encapsulation, and multicast.
sections.plainLanguage: IPoIB selects the InfiniBand transport mode supported by every InfiniBand element. This lets IP use a consistent transport across the fabric.

sections.title: An IPoIB Link and Its Broadcast Group
sections.content:
An IPoIB link is an abstract group defined by its members and shared settings, including a partition key (P_Key), link MTU, and queue key (Q_Key). The physical layout does not define the link boundary.

A broadcast-GID must exist for an IPoIB subnet to form. Every IPoIB interface MUST join that group as a FullMember. The join returns settings such as the MTU and Q_Key, and the group provides the link-layer broadcast needed by protocols such as ARP.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPoIB link consists of interfaces that join the same configured broadcast group. That group also supplies shared settings needed to send packets.

sections.title: The Encapsulation Header
sections.content:
Each IP and ARP datagram carried over InfiniBand begins with a four-octet header. Its Type field identifies the following protocol using an ETHER TYPE value; its Reserved field MUST be zero when sent and is ignored when received.

The defined Type values are 0x800 for IPv4, 0x806 for ARP, 0x8035 for RARP, and 0x86DD for IPv6. An implementation MUST handle packets with or without a Global Routing Header because InfiniBand uses that header in some, but not all, paths.
sections.plainLanguage: A short header tells the receiver which network protocol follows. The packet may also include an InfiniBand routing header, depending on its path.

sections.title: MTU and IPv6 Interface Identifiers
sections.content:
InfiniBand components support several maximum payload sizes. Each IPoIB implementation MUST support an IPoIB-link MTU of 2044 octets, which leaves room for the four-octet encapsulation header within a 2048-octet link MTU. Other MTUs MAY be supported.

An IPv6 interface identifier can be based on the InfiniBand port's EUI-64 GUID or, within one InfiniBand subnet, a 16-bit LID. A LID may change after a reboot. The RFC recommends constructing a link-local address from the port's EUI-64 identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Every implementation must support a common minimum packet size for the link. IPv6 can use an identifier based on the InfiniBand port, while a local LID may change after restart.

sections.title: Unicast Address Resolution
sections.content:
IPv4 uses ARP and IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery to resolve network addresses. The InfiniBand link-layer address is 20 octets: eight reserved bits, a 24-bit queue-pair number, and a 16-octet GID. IP traffic to an interface MUST be directed to its specified queue pair.

Some link information is obtained separately: the Q_Key comes from joining the broadcast group, while the P_Key is configured. Because a queue-pair number may change after a reboot or interface reset, implementations are RECOMMENDED to revalidate ARP caches periodically.
sections.plainLanguage: The link-layer address identifies both an InfiniBand endpoint and its queue pair. Since the queue-pair number can change, old address entries may need checking again.

sections.title: Mapping and Sending Multicast
sections.content:
InfiniBand multicast uses Multicast Global Identifiers (MGIDs). IPoIB builds an MGID from the IP multicast address and the link's P_Key. The signature is 0x401B for IPv4 and 0x601B for IPv6; IPv4's limited broadcast maps to the broadcast-GID.

An InfiniBand multicast group must be created and joined before it can carry packets. A sender joins as a SendOnlyNonMember or FullMember, depending on whether it also needs to receive. An IP multicast router can emulate promiscuous multicast by joining each matching group as a NonMember and watching for new groups.
sections.plainLanguage: IP multicast addresses map to InfiniBand group identifiers. A port must join a group before sending to it or receiving its packets.

sections.title: Resource and Security Considerations
sections.content:
InfiniBand multicast operations can fail when groups, joins, or queue-pair resources are unavailable. Some failures may not be visible to senders. Implementations SHOULD log errors, and administrators should preserve sufficient multicast resources.

The RFC notes that multicast networks can permit identity spoofing, forged traffic, or eavesdropping; higher layers must provide countermeasures when needed. Operating-system controls MUST protect link setup operations, and controlled Q_Keys SHOULD be used to prevent unprivileged software from fabricating IP datagrams.
sections.plainLanguage: Multicast setup can fail silently if the fabric lacks resources, so implementations should record errors. Higher layers must protect traffic when multicast identity or privacy matters.
